To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the crystal structure of the i-type lyozyme-inhibitor complex from A. hydrophila reveals the inhibitory mechanism at the atomic level and that the interface is formed by a single `key-lock' mechanism.

the crystal structure of the i-type lyoszyme inhibitor from A. hydrophila (Aerolysin) has been determined at 1.24 Å resolution and the inhibitory mechanism is explained at the atomic level, and that this mechanism is similar to the mechanism of other classes of lysozyme inhibitors.

the crystal structure of the complex of the Aeromonas hydrophilai-type lysozymeinhibitor (PliI) with Meretrix luso-ria i-type lysozymeresolves to 1.24 Å resolution and that the structure explains the inhibitory mechanism at the atomic level by revealing that the PliI inhibitor forms an extensive interface of a double `keylock' type, resulting in efficient inhibition of lysozyme activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of bacterial lytic enzymes and their inhibitors.
the development of novel antibiotics.
the development of a new generation of antibacterial drugs based on the inhibition of lysozymes from pathogenic bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all known inhibitors of c-, g- and i-type lyases are of a `key-lock' design, with the inhibitor binding to the substrate-binding groove in a way that prevents the enzyme from catalysis.
the structure of the PliA-Ah complex represents the first example of the inhibition mechanism for the PliI class of lysozyme inhibitors.
the PliI inhibitors bind to the substrate lysozyme by forming an extensive interface that is composed of two distinct `key-lock' regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the structure of the Pli-Ah/lysozyme complex reveals a `key-lock' interaction between a lysozyme and its specific inhibitor, and provides a structural basis for the rational design of new antimicrobial agents.
we have discovered a new class of inhibitors of bacterial lysozymes and we have solved the structure of the complex between a representative member of this class and its target enzyme.

the PliI inhibitor is an example of a protein that evolved to bind a protein target with high affinity, and the structural data reported here provide the first explanation at the atomic level of the inhibitory mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure of the proteinacious inhibitor PliI-Aeromonas hydrophilia in complex with its substrate lysozyme is solved to 1.24 A resolution.

the PliI inhibitor from Aeromonus hydrophila (Ah) binds to its substrate lysozyme (Lyso) from Meretrix Lusoria (Ml) in a `key-lock' fashion, with the `ridge' formed from the loops 3, 4, and 5 of PliI interacting with the substrate-binding groove in the Lyso.
the structural data on lyzoyme-inhibitor complexes provide a basis for rational design of a new class antibacterial agents.
